opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It really was a turning point for me.

I'd been working on a problem about the symmetries of black holes: how certain equations that describe perturbations around a black hole hide structure that isn't obvious at first. It's the kind of problem where you spend days, sometimes weeks, playing with the math before you see the pattern. I knew the answer because my collaborators and I had worked it out, and it hadn't been easy. So I gave it to the model mostly as a test. I honestly expected it to fail, or to produce something that sounded plausible but fell apart.

It didn't fail. The first attempt didn't quite get there, but when I gave it a simpler warm-up version and then came back to the real problem, it reasoned through it and found the symmetry. Watching that happen in real time was a little dizzying. This wasn't looking something up. It was the kind of creative step I'd thought of as the core of what a theoretical physicist does.

My reaction was something like: this changes things. If a tool can do in minutes part of what took us a long time, then the way science gets done is about to shift, maybe dramatically. And I didn't want to watch that from the sidelines. I wanted to help figure out how to use these systems well in physics: where they're reliable, where they're not, how to check them, and how to pair them with human intuition so we can tackle problems we couldn't reach before.

There's also a sense of responsibility. Scientists who understand these problems deeply need to be involved in shaping how these tools work, so we end up with something that accelerates discovery rather than something we just trust blindly. Once I'd seen what it could do, staying out felt like the wrong choice.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes the problem as difficult and says it took him and his collaborators a long time, but does not say it was at the edge of Alex’s own abilities.

r003.rationale: He says the result made him want to help shape and use AI in physics and that staying out felt like the wrong choice.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, to give some context, this was a problem I'd been carrying around for a long time. In my work on black holes, you often run into these hidden symmetries in the geometry near the horizon, and there was one particular question about the structure of those symmetries that I'd really struggled with. I'd spent months on it. I'd asked colleagues, I'd tried different approaches, and I had a kind of intuition for what the answer should look like, but I couldn't nail it down. It was the sort of thing where you suspect the answer exists, you can almost feel its shape, but the technical path to it keeps slipping away.

And then, somewhat on a whim, I gave the problem to one of these models. I didn't expect much. I'd used earlier systems and they were fine for summarizing a paper or cleaning up some code, but they'd fall apart on anything genuinely hard. This time was different. It didn't just produce something plausible-sounding. It actually worked through the structure, it found the right way to organize the calculation, and it arrived at a result that I then checked by hand and that held up. It was correct, and it was elegant.

That was a strange moment for me, honestly. There's a part of you that's thrilled, because you finally have the answer. And there's another part that's a little unsettled, because the thing that just happened was supposed to be the hard, creative, human part of being a theoretical physicist. That's the part I'd built my identity around.

So why did that push me toward AI rather than just making me a happy user of it? I think it was two things. The first is that I realized the pace of this was faster than I'd internalized. If a model could do that today, then the questions I care about, the deep questions about gravity and quantum mechanics, might be approached in a totally different way within a few years. And I wanted to understand that from the inside, not read about it afterward. The second is more about responsibility. These systems are starting to touch the frontier of actual scientific knowledge, and I think it matters enormously that people who know what rigorous science looks like, who know what a real proof or a real calculation requires, are in the room helping shape how these tools get built and evaluated. I didn't want to just be a passenger on that. I wanted to be useful to it.

astra-6.text:
Because it changed my sense of what these systems could contribute to science. When you’ve spent a lot of time thinking about a difficult problem, you develop a feeling for where the hard part is. Seeing AI get through that hard part in a problem I understood deeply made the possibility very concrete for me.

And that’s an extraordinary thing to encounter as a scientist. The point is to understand nature, and suddenly there’s a new tool that might help us answer questions we’ve struggled with. I wanted to understand how far that could go, where it would fail, and how to work with it. It felt like something I needed to participate in.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it changed my sense of what was possible. When you’ve spent a long time wrestling with a problem, you have a very personal understanding of what makes it difficult. Seeing AI solve it makes the progress feel concrete in a way that no benchmark can. This was something I cared about, and suddenly there was a new way to make progress on it.

That made me want to be involved. If these systems could help us tackle questions about black holes, what else could they help us understand? I wanted to explore that—and help figure out how to make them useful for doing science.
